hook_text: Durban and Port Nolloth are on the same latitude. One gets about 1 000 mm of rain. The other gets about 60.
clip_script: Draw a line across South Africa at about thirty degrees south. On the east end: Durban, warm, sticky, green, with about one thousand millimetres of rain a year. On the west end: Port Nolloth, cool, grey, foggy, with about sixty. Same distance from the equator. Both at sea level. So what is different? The sea. Past Durban rushes the warm Agulhas Current from the tropics. It heats the air and fills it with moisture, and the moisture becomes rain. Past Port Nolloth flows the cold Benguela, with icy water welling up from the deep. It chills the air from below, so it stays still and dry. No rain, just fog. But that cold water is full of nutrients, and the west coast is one of the richest fishing grounds on earth.
visual_style: A whiteboard map with a red arrow flowing down the east coast and a blue arrow flowing up the west coast, rain clouds over Durban and a fog bank over Port Nolloth.
pacing: A sharp contrast up front, a reveal, then a twist about fish.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and follow the currents around the coast.
